|- class="mergedtoprow" title="Land/länder där objektet ligger" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |[[Country]] |[[Japan]] |- class="mergedrow" title="Region(er) där objektet ligger" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |Region |[[Chūbu region|Chūbu]] |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- class="mergedtoprow" title="Lokalisering" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |City |[[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture|Ishikawa prefecture]] |- class="mergedrow" title="Geografiska koordinater" | style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |coordinates |[//geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?language=sv&pagename=Sug%C5%8Disobe-jinja¶ms=36.3130_N_136.3208_E_type:landmark_region:JP 36°18′47″N 136°19′15″Ö﻿ / ﻿36.3130°N 136.3208°Ö﻿ / 36.3130; 136.3208] |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- class="mergedtoprow" title="Grundläggningsdatum" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |Address |585 e.Kr. |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- title="Officiell eller betydande webbplats" | colspan="2" style="text-align: center;" |'''[[Website]]: ''' http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ |} {{Expand Japanese}} [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja, torii on street.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|{{Center|Torii}}]] '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]], on the Daishōji grounds. It was mentioned in the engishiki of 927 and held the shakaku rank of kokuhei shōsha, which is the national shrine of the 3rd rank. During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. Locally, it is referred to as "Shikichi Tenjin" or "Sugō Tenjin." == Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto. There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami. == History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the engishiki jinmyōchō, a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as shōsha, and it held the second highest rank (ni no miya) in Kaga province. The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to shōshii no ge, an upper fourth rank, lower degree. The Heike monogatari, a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that Minamoto no Yoshinaka donated to the shrine. During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of Kitano Tenmangū, and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time. == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja. In 1987, Ishikawa Prefecture designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.. [[User:Redstar0005|Redstar0005]] [[User talk:Redstar0005|talk to me!]] 21:45, 10 December 2023 (UTC)}} ---- Merge this content to the proper page [[simple:Sugo Ishibe Shrine]] and fix [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Tsurugi Shrine]] too and [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Oagata Shrine]] {{complex}} ---- {{infobox shinto shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Sugoisobe-jinja, Haiden from Afar - 2020.jpg | caption = Haiden |map_type=Japan| coordinates = {{coordinates|36.3130|N|136.3208|E}} | deity = Sugōisobe no Kami. ([[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]], [[Ugayafukiaezu]]) possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]]. It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178. . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}} The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide. == Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto. There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami. == History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]]. The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}} The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}} During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time. In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}.{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}} In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage. === Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity. === Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being. An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds. Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes. === Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life. A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers. === Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea. == The area == File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=本殿|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-1.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-2.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-1.jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-2.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine == References == {{reflist}} {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[simple:{{PAGENAME}}]] [[ja:菅生石部神社]] [[sv:Sugōisobe-jinja]][[ja:菅生石部神社]][[simple:Sugo Ishibe Shrine]][[en:Draft:Sugōisobe Shrine]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Draft articles]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[fr:User:{{PAGENAME}}]][[simple:User:{{PAGENAME}}]] }}

Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}} The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}} During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time. In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}.{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}} In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage. === Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity. === Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being. An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds. Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes. === Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life. A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers. === Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea. == The area == File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=本殿|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-1.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-2.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-1.jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-2.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine == References == {{reflist}} {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[simple:{{PAGENAME}}]] [[ja:菅生石部神社]] [[sv:Sugōisobe-jinja]][[ja:菅生石部神社]][[simple:Sugo Ishibe Shrine]][[en:Draft:Sugōisobe Shrine]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Draft articles]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[fr:User:{{PAGENAME}}]][[simple:User:{{PAGENAME}}]] }}

In 1987, Ishikawa Prefecture designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.. {{Cite web |url=http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka5.html#gonganshinji |title=加賀市教育委員会（文化財保護課） |access-date=2023-04-16 |archive-date=2023-04-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416222113/http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka5.html#gonganshinji |url-status=dead }} == The area == File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=本殿|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from outside.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from inside.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Hakusan (1).jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Inari.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine == References == [[Category:Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]]

{{infobox shinto shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Sugoisobe-jinja, Haiden from Afar - 2020.jpg | caption = Haiden |map_type=Japan| coordinates = {{coordinates|36.3130|N|136.3208|E}} | deity = Sugōisobe no Kami. ([[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]], [[Ugayafukiaezu]])
possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]].<ref name=":1" /> It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927<ref name="nussbaum178">[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />
It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

{{infobox shinto shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Sugoisobe-jinja, Haiden from Afar - 2020.jpg | caption = Haiden |map_type=Japan| coordinates = {{coordinates|36.3130|N|136.3208|E}} | deity = Sugōisobe no Kami. ([[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]], [[Ugayafukiaezu]])
possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]].<ref name=":1" /> It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927<ref name="nussbaum178">[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />
It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />
== The area == <gallery> File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=本殿|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-1.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-2.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-1.jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-2.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine </gallery>

|- class="mergedtoprow" title="Land/länder där objektet ligger" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |[[Country]] |[[Japan]] |- class="mergedrow" title="Region(er) där objektet ligger" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |Region |[[Chūbu region|Chūbu]] |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- class="mergedtoprow" title="Lokalisering" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |City |[[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture|Ishikawa prefecture]] |- class="mergedrow" title="Geografiska koordinater" | style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |coordinates |[//geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?language=sv&pagename=Sug%C5%8Disobe-jinja¶ms=36.3130_N_136.3208_E_type:landmark_region:JP 36°18′47″N 136°19′15″Ö﻿ / ﻿36.3130°N 136.3208°Ö﻿ / 36.3130; 136.3208] |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- class="mergedtoprow" title="Grundläggningsdatum" ! style="white-space: nowrap; text-align: left;" |Address |585 e.Kr. |- class="mergedrow" |- class="mergedrow" style="height: 0.2em;" | colspan="2" | |- title="Officiell eller betydande webbplats" | colspan="2" style="text-align: center;" |'''[[Website]]: ''' http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ |} {{Expand Japanese}} [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja, torii on street.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|{{Center|Torii}}]] '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]], on the Daishōji grounds. It was mentioned in the engishiki of 927 and held the shakaku rank of kokuhei shōsha, which is the national shrine of the 3rd rank. During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. Locally, it is referred to as "Shikichi Tenjin" or "Sugō Tenjin." == Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto. There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami. == History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the engishiki jinmyōchō, a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as shōsha, and it held the second highest rank (ni no miya) in Kaga province. The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to shōshii no ge, an upper fourth rank, lower degree. The Heike monogatari, a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that Minamoto no Yoshinaka donated to the shrine. During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of Kitano Tenmangū, and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time. == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja. In 1987, Ishikawa Prefecture designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.. {{Cite web |url=http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka5.html#gonganshinji |title=加賀市教育委員会（文化財保護課） |access-date=2023-04-16 |archive-date=2023-04-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416222113/http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka5.html#gonganshinji |url-status=dead }} == The area == File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=本殿|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from outside.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from inside.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Hakusan (1).jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Inari.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine == References == [[Category:Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]]

(2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />
It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

[[別表神社]] | 創建=（伝）[[用明天皇]]元年（[[585年]]） | 本殿=[[流造]] | 例祭=[[2月10日]] | 地図={{Location map|Japan Ishikawa|label=菅生
石部神社|coordinates= {{coord2|36|18|46.9|N|136|19|14.9|E|}}|position=right|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=13|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|frame-height=250|coord={{coord|36|18|46.9|N|136|19|14.9|E}}}} }} [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja, torii on street.jpg|thumb|250px|right|{{center|鳥居}}]] '''菅生石部神社'''（すごういそべじんじゃ）は、[[石川県]][[加賀市]]大聖寺敷地にある[[神社]]。[[式内社]]、[[加賀国]][[一宮|二宮]]で、[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[国幣小社]]。現在は[[神社本庁]]の[[別表神社]]。通称を「敷地天神」・「菅生天神」とも。 == 祭神 == 現在の祭神は「菅生石部神」となっており、これは[[ホオリ|天津日高日子穗穗出見命]]、[[トヨタマヒメ|豐玉毘賣命]]、[[ウガヤフキアエズ|鵜葺草葺不合命]]の三柱の総称としている。 祭神については諸説あり、[[スクナビコナ|少彦名神]]とする説もある。菅生石部神の本体三柱も、元は祭神の諸説の一つであった。 == 歴史 == 社伝によれば、[[用明天皇]]元年（[[585年]]）、この地で疾病が流行したとき、宮中で祀られていた菅生石部神が勧請されたのに始まるという。[[延喜式神名帳]]では小社に列し、加賀国二宮とされた。古来より朝廷・武門からの崇敬が篤く、[[天慶]]3年には[[正四位下]]の[[神階]]が授けられた。『[[平家物語]]』巻七には、[[源義仲|木曾義仲]]が当社へ「のみ（野美）の庄」を寄進したとの記述がある。中世には、一帯は[[北野天満宮]]の社領となっていた。「天神」の通称はそこからきたものであり、現在もその名残で境内に牛の像が残っている。 [[明治]]29年（[[1896年]]）に国幣小社に昇格した。 京都の[[敷地神社]]（わら天神）は、当社からの勧請と伝える。 == 境内 == File:Sugoisobe-jinja, honden-2.jpg|本殿 File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shaden.jpg|拝殿 File:Sugoisobe-jinja, kaguraden.jpg|神楽殿 File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shamusho.jpg|社務所 File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from outside.jpg|神門（加賀市指定文化財） File:Sugoisobe-jinja, shinmon from inside.jpg|神門（境内側） File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Hakusan (1).jpg|白山社 File:Sugoisobe-jinja, keidaisha for Inari.jpg|敷地稲荷社 == 祭事 == 毎年[[2月10日]]の[[例祭]]では、「[[竹割り祭り]]」の異名を持つ御願神事（ごんがんしんじ）が行われる。御願神事は1987年に石川県指定無形民俗文化財となる[http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka5.html#gonganshinji 加賀市教育委員会（文化財保護課）]。 == 文化財 == === 重要文化財（国指定） === * 蒔絵角赤手箱（附 文章1巻）（工芸品） - [[東京国立博物館]]寄託。1900年（明治33年）4月7日指定{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|5245|蒔絵角赤手箱}}。 * 正親町天皇宸翰御詠草 永禄四年八月十五日夜三条西公条点（書跡・典籍） - [[石川県立美術館]]寄託。1900年（明治33年）4月7日指定{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|7612|正親町天皇宸翰御詠草}}。 === 石川県指定文化財 === * 無形民俗文化財 ** 御願神事 - 1987年（昭和62年）3月23日指定[http://www.kaga.ed.jp/bunka7.html 指定文化財一覧]（加賀市ホームページ）。。 === 加賀市指定文化財 === * 有形文化財 ** 菅生石部神社神門（建造物） - 1976年（昭和51年）7月19日指定。 ** 藤原共方1巻 左聴等1巻 前田利長3巻 前田利常1巻 前田利治利明1巻（古文書） - 加賀市美術館寄託。1959年（昭和34年）7月13日指定。 ** 洲崎久利筆縁起書1巻 前田利明筆縁起書1巻（典籍） - 加賀市美術館寄託。1959年（昭和34年）7月13日指定。 ** 社禄書（足利義持 山口玄蕃 前田利長 前田利常） 4巻（古文書） - 加賀市美術館寄託。1959年（昭和34年）7月13日指定。 ** 絹本著色天神画像 伝狩野元信筆（絵画） - 加賀市美術館寄託。1959年（昭和34年）7月13日指定。 ** 絹本著色天神画像 伝土佐光信筆（絵画） - 加賀市美術館寄託。1959年（昭和34年）7月13日指定。 ** 絹本著色寿老人図 伝周文筆（絵画） - In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]].<ref name=":1" /> It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927<ref name="nussbaum178">[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />

=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />

=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]].<ref name=":1" /> It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927<ref name="nussbaum178">[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting Festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />
It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == Festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar Festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />

----
Merge this content to the proper page [[simple:Sugōisobe Shrine]] and fix [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Tsurugi Shrine]] too and [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Oagata Shrine]] {{complex}}[[simple:Sugōisobe Shrine]] {{User:Immanuelle/Promising Draft}} ----
{{infobox shinto shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Sugoisobe-jinja, Haiden from Afar - 2020.jpg | caption = Haiden |map_type=Japan| coordinates = {{coordinates|36.3130|N|136.3208|E}} | deity = Sugōisobe no Kami. ([[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]], [[Ugayafukiaezu]])
possibly [[Sukunabikona]] | website = http://www.tenjin.or.tv/ | links = [[ja:菅生石部神社]] }} '''Sugōisobe-jinja''' (菅生石部神社) is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Kaga, Ishikawa|Kaga]], [[Ishikawa Prefecture]].<ref name=":1" /> It was mentioned in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] of 927<ref name="nussbaum178">[[Louis-Frédéric|Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric]]. (2005). [https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&pg=PA178&dq= "''Engi-shiki''"] in ''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 178.</ref> . [[File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_torii-1.jpg|right|thumb|250x250px|Torii]]During the feudal era, it was of the second-highest rank in [[Kaga Province]]. Currently, the shrine is directly controlled by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].
It is located a mile from [[Daishōji Station]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BIw0AAAAIAAJ&q=Sugo+Ishibe |title=Musashino |date=1914 |language=en}}</ref>
The shrine is renowned for hosting the Takewari Matsuri also known as the Bamboo Splitting festival. This traditional event, rich, in heritage occurs annually on February 10. Attracts attendees and onlookers from far and wide.<ref name=":1" />
It is similarly named but not related to the shrine {{nihongo|{{ill|Isobe Shrine|ja|石部神社}}|石部神社}} located in [[Komatsu, Ishikawa]].
== Worshiped ''kami'' == The deity worshipped at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine is Sugōisobe no Kami. This name represents three deities, namely [[Hoori]], [[Toyotama-hime]] no Mikoto, and [[Ugayafukiaezu]] no Mikoto.
There are several theories about the true identity of the deity at Sugōisobe-jinja shrine. Some scholars suggest that the deity is actually [[Sukunabikona]], rather than Sugōisobe no Kami.
== History == According to legend, Sugōisobe no Kami was brought to the area from the imperial court in 585 when a serious illness spread throughout the region. The shrine was recorded in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]], a record of all shrines in Japan compiled in 927, as a shōsha<ref name="nussbaum178" />, and it held the second highest rank ([[Ninomiya]]) in [[Kaga Province|Kaga province]].
The shrine was highly respected by the imperial court and the samurai class, and in 940, the deity was elevated to {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=shōshii no ge|ja|神階|en:draft}}, a high {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|ja|神階|en:draft}}. Higher rank meant more lands were given to the shrine and it became wealthier and more powerful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Basic Terms of Shinto: Shinkai |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/bts/bts_s.html |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>
The [[The Tale of the Heike|Heike monogatari]], a Japanese epic of the 12th century, also mentioned that [[Minamoto no Yoshinaka]] donated to the shrine.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yoshikawa |first1=Eiji |title=The Heike Story: A Modern Translation of the Classic Japanese Tale of Love and War |last2=Bhowmik |first2=Davinder |date=2011-04-10 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=978-4-8053-1044-1 |edition=Reprint |language=English |translator-last=Uramatsu |translator-first=Fuki Wooyenaka}}</ref>
During the Middle Ages, the entire area was incorporated into the territory of [[Kitano Tenmangū]], and Sugōisobe-jinja came to be known as "Tenjin" due to the god worshipped there. A bull statue, [[Shinshi|associated]] with [[Sugawara no Michizane|Tenjin]], still stands as a reminder of that time.
In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />
== The area == <gallery> File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_honden-2.jpg|alt=main hall|main shrine File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shaden.jpg|alt=拝殿|worship hall File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_kaguraden.jpg|alt=神楽殿|Kaguraden File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shamusho.jpg|alt=社務所|shrine office File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-1.jpg|alt=神門（加賀市指定文化財）|Shinmon Gate (Kaga City Designated Cultural Property) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_shinmon-2.jpg|alt=神門（境内側）|Shrine gate (inside the precincts) File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-1.jpg|alt=白山社|Hakusansha File:Sugoisobe-jinja,_keidaisha-2.jpg|alt=敷地稲荷社|Site Inari Shrine </gallery>
== References == {{reflist}} {{Draft categories| [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[en:Sugōisobe Shrine]][[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Prefecturally designated intangible folk cultural property]] [[Category:Ishikawa Prefecture]] [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[simple:{{PAGENAME}}]] [[ja:菅生石部神社]] [[sv:Sugōisobe-jinja]][[ja:菅生石部神社]][[simple:Sugo Ishibe Shrine]][[en:Draft:Sugōisobe Shrine]] [[Category:Kokuhei Shōsha]] [[en:Sugōisobe Shrine]][[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Original pages]] [[Category:original pages]][[Category:original pages]] [[Category:Original pages]][[simple:user:immanuelle/Sugōisobe Shrine]][[category:original pages]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from wikipedia5]][[en:Sugōisobe Shrine]][[Category:Pages and Categories from wikipedia5]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]][[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[en:Sugōisobe Shrine]][[fr:User:{{PAGENAME}}]][[simple:User:{{PAGENAME}}]] }}

In 1875 it had a unique Shinmon gate built for it in a semi-european style with three stories.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bocking |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MWGQAgAAQBAJ&dq=Sug%C5%8Disobe&pg=PT264 |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2005-09-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-79738-6 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=126}} == festivals == Every year on February 10th, the Gongan Shinji festival, also known as "Takewari-matsuri," is held at Sugōisobe-jinja<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2023-12-07|title=Gogan shinji {{!}} 國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207005240/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9343|access-date=2024-04-08|website=web.archive.org}}</ref>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Peculiar festivals of Hokuriku {{!}} festival {{!}} Hokuriku Tales |url=https://monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org/en/hotspring/festival/index.html |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=monogatari.hokuriku-imageup.org}}</ref> In 1987, [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] designated the festival as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.
=== Event Overview === The festival kicks off with a service held within the shrine grounds. Subsequently the atmosphere transforms into a celebration of energy and excitement. Young parishioners called ujiko from areas such as Shikiji and Oka don traditional garb, for the festivity. They don underclothes, hakama trousers, white tabi socks and sandals to symbolize purity and solidarity.<ref name=":1" />
=== Ceremonial Activities === After getting dressed in their attire participants head out onto the snow covered temple grounds known as keidai carrying bamboo poles measuring over two meters. Demonstrating strength and unity they vigorously strike the shrines structures with the bamboo sticks as a gesture to drive away energies and safeguard the communitys well being.<ref name=":1" />
An hour after this bamboo ritual a spirited tug of war contest unfolds.<ref name=":1" />
Participants engage in an activity involving a rope often compared to a massive snake to demonstrate their strength and resilience. The highlight of this event is tossing the "rope snake”, off the Shikiji Bridge into the Daishōji River symbolizing the release of negativity and the embrace of vibes.<ref name=":1" />
=== Cultural Importance === Onlookers and devotees at the Sugōisobe Shrine eagerly gather pieces of bamboo used during the ceremony. These bamboo fragments hold significance as talismans believed to ward off evil and bring luck. Additionally participants receive chopsticks crafted from the bamboo, known as goganbashi further integrating the festivals importance into life.<ref name=":1" />
A unique custom involves fishermen from the Shiotani area who retrieve the rope snake from the river. They believe that incorporating strands of this rope into their towropes will ensure a catch highlighting their belief in the festivals symbols protective and auspicious powers.<ref name=":1" />
=== Historical Roots === The Takewari Matsuri has its origins in a prayer by Emperor Tenmu for favor. The term "gogan shinji" linked with this festival reflects its background, with "gan" signifying prayer or plea.<ref name=":1" />
